title: The coat (Genesis 37:1–11)
hook: a favorite son, a special coat, and dreams of sheaves bowing down

segments.voice: Yesterday, Rachel dies on the road, and is buried where her children would pass. Your line was she weeps for her children. Did you reach a mother? Today, her firstborn. Day sixty-five.

Every family with more than one child knows this one. The kid who gets the later curfew. The one whose photo is bigger on the fridge. Parents swear they don't have a favorite, and the kids always know. In Jacob's house, nobody even pretends. Joseph is seventeen. He's Rachel's son, and Rachel is gone. He tends the flocks with his older brothers, and he brings back bad reports about them to their father. And one day Jacob gives Joseph a gift. Only Joseph. Something the brothers see every single day. Today: the coat.
screen: `PARENTS SAY THEY HAVE NO FAVORITE.` → `JOSEPH, SEVENTEEN, RACHEL'S SON.` → `A GIFT FOR ONLY ONE.`

segments.voice: The Torah says it straight out: "Now Israel loved Joseph more than all his children, because he was the son of his old age; and he made him a coat of many colours." Many colors: that's how the old translations put it, and it's how the musical puts it too. But here's a secret. Nobody is sure what the Hebrew means. The words are ketonet passim. Ketonet is a tunic. Passim is the puzzle. The ancient Greek translation guessed many colors. Others think it means long sleeves, reaching to the palms and the ankles, a coat for someone who doesn't have to work in the fields. The only other place the phrase appears in the whole Bible is on a king's daughter. Whatever it looked like, the brothers understood it perfectly. The text says they hated him, and couldn't speak a peaceful word to him. Then Joseph has dreams, and tells them. Sheaves of grain in a field, and all the brothers' sheaves bow down to his. Then the sun, the moon and eleven stars bow down to him. Even Jacob scolds him for that one. But the text says his father kept the saying in mind. The Talmud draws a lesson from the coat that parents still quote. A person should never favor one child over the others, it says, because for a little bit of fine wool that Jacob gave Joseph beyond his brothers, the brothers grew jealous, and in the end our ancestors went down into Egypt. The whole story of slavery in Egypt, the Talmud says, begins with a coat.
screen: `ISRAEL LOVED JOSEPH MORE.` · `KETONET PASSIM: NOBODY IS SURE.` · `SHEAVES, SUN, MOON AND STARS BOW.` · `A LITTLE WOOL, AND DOWN TO EGYPT.` · then, large: `HE LOVED JOSEPH MORE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice a favor that breeds resentment. Settle, and breathe. Think of a place in your life where someone gets a little more. More attention, more patience, more credit. Maybe it's you who gets it. Maybe it's you who watches someone else get it. Notice what it does to the people around it. You don't have to fix anything. Just see it clearly, the way the brothers saw that coat every day. The bell holds the time.
The coat. Ketonet passim, a gift for the favorite son. Nobody's sure what it looked like, but everyone knew what it meant.
Your line: favorites cost. Today, give a little of your attention to someone who usually gets less of it. Day sixty-five.

howItsDone: The Joseph story is read in synagogue over four weeks each winter, and Jewish parents and teachers often cite the Talmud's lesson from the coat about treating children evenly.

original.note: Hebrew: Joseph's coat. ketonet is a tunic; the meaning of passim is uncertain.

trapdoor: what you thought: a coat of many colors.
what it means: a gift that marked one son as the favorite, and set the brothers against him.
what a scholar hears: ketonet passim, uncertain. the Septuagint guessed many colors; others read long sleeves. the phrase recurs only in 2 Samuel 13:18.

sources.quoted: Now Israel loved Joseph more than all his children, because he was the son of his old age; and he made him a coat of many colours.

notes: Genesis 37:3 JPS 1917 wording: confirm (British 'colours' kept inside the quotation).

Ketonet passim: Septuagint 'poikilos' (many-colored); 'long sleeves/reaching to palms and ankles' reading (Genesis Rabbah and modern scholarship). Only other occurrence: 2 Samuel 13:18–19 (Tamar). Confirm.
Shabbat 10b paraphrased (two sela's weight of fine wool). Confirm.
The reference to 'the musical' (Joseph and the Amazing Technicolor Dreamcoat) is unnamed; confirm it's appropriate.
